transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, um… I’m here because these flashes keep hitting me out of nowhere. Like I’ll just be standing at a pickup counter, waiting on an order — you know how some places make you wait forever and everybody’s kind of crowding around — and suddenly it’s like I’m back in that holding room. Crowded, loud… seeing that fight start, hearing everybody getting shoved up against the wall. It just comes in like I’m there again, not here.
What happens right before these flashes hit you?

Usually it’s something like… I’m waiting around somewhere, like at a pickup counter, people pressed in too close, noise bouncing around, everybody kind of impatient. And then it just flips on me. I’m not thinking about it on purpose — one second I’m there waiting for food, and the next it’s like I’m back in that crowded holding room, seeing the fight start and hearing people getting shoved into the wall.

It’s weird because pickup counters are already chaotic, you know, drivers cutting in, staff yelling names, phones going off… I do that all day, so I can’t exactly avoid it. But yeah, right before it happens, it’s usually that crowded, loud waiting feeling.
Do you find yourself trying to avoid places or situations that might trigger these flashes?

Yeah… yeah, I guess I am. I mean, I keep telling myself I’m just “being smart with routes,” like with traffic and construction and all that — this city’s a mess after five anyway — but really I’ve been turning down night runs if they take me anywhere near that detention building.

And during the day I’ll take this stupid long loop around town just so I don’t have to pass it. Costs me time, gas, everything. I know it doesn’t make sense, but when I even think about going by there, or if somebody asks me what happened, it’s like my body thinks I’m back in that room again. So… yeah, I avoid it. I try not to talk about it either.
Do you avoid other things besides places that might trigger these flashes?

Yeah… I mean, besides the actual place, I avoid talking about it. Like if somebody asks why I won’t take certain runs, I’ll make some excuse about traffic or parking or whatever. And the night runs too — I’ve been turning those down if they go anywhere near that detention building.

It’s stupid because I’m losing money doing it, and I already spend enough on gas — my car’s been making this rattling sound too, which is a whole other thing — but I just… I can’t make myself go near there, or get into what happened, because it feels like I’m right back in that room.
Do you have trouble sleeping at night?

Yeah… sleep is kind of gone lately. I’ll pass out for maybe an hour, two if I’m lucky, and then I’m up again because of some dream about being back in that cell, or I hear a door slam in the dream and I wake up like it actually happened.

And then I just lie there. I mean, I used to be able to crash after driving all day — especially with this job, because you’re in and out of the car nonstop, dealing with restaurants, apartments with no parking, all that — but now by morning I feel wrecked. Like too wiped out to trust myself driving my route.
Do you often feel on edge or easily startled?

Yeah… yeah, definitely. Like every little sound sets me off now. A radio crackling, a siren going by, some door slamming in a hallway — I jump like somebody’s about to rush me.

And then it doesn’t just go away. My heart keeps pounding, and I’m sitting there trying to act normal, like I’m just checking my phone or fixing my delivery bag or whatever. Sometimes I have to pull over when I’m driving, or step outside if I’m in a building, just to get myself back down. It’s… it’s embarrassing, honestly.
Do you try to push away memories of what happened in that holding room?

Yeah… I try to shove it out of my head, but it doesn’t really work. I’ll change the subject if someone asks, or I’ll make up some reason I can’t take a run.

I’ve been turning down night runs and taking the long way around town, which is ridiculous because the long way burns more gas — and gas is already, you know, insane — but I just can’t make myself go near that detention building. Or even talk about what happened in that holding room without feeling like I’m right back there.
Do you often think that you're to blame for what happened in that holding room or that you're worthless because of it?

I don’t… I don’t know if I’d put it like that. Worthless sounds kind of big.

I mean, I do keep replaying stuff, like what I should’ve said or not said, and then I’ll get off on this whole thing about how people look at you after something like that — or maybe they don’t even notice, I don’t know. My boss just cares if the delivery gets there, honestly. He’ll text three question marks if I’m five minutes late, like that helps anybody.

But blame… I’m not sure. I haven’t really sat there thinking, “this is all my fault,” exactly. It’s more like I don’t want to think about it long enough to figure out what I think.
Do you feel guilty about what happened in that holding room?

Guilty… I don’t know. I mean, I keep trying to figure out if that’s the word for it, but then my brain goes somewhere else.

Like, I’ll think maybe I should’ve done something different, and then I’m thinking about the route I had that night, and whether I should’ve taken the expressway, because honestly traffic has been a mess lately and dispatch keeps acting like we can teleport. And then I’m like… wait, what were we talking about?

So, guilty? I’m not sure. I don’t really have a clear answer for that.
Do you think you're a bad person because of what happened in that holding room?

I don’t… I don’t think I’ve been walking around saying, “I’m a bad person,” no.

It’s more like my head gets noisy and then I end up thinking about totally other stuff, like whether people can tell something’s off with me, or if I’m acting weird at work, and then I’m checking my phone because dispatch is always blowing it up. Sorry — that’s not really what you asked.

So… bad person? I’m not sure. I don’t think that’s exactly the thought I’m having.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I’m not sure. I mean, “enjoy” is kind of… I don’t know, I haven’t really been keeping score.

Like, I used to have things I’d do when I got off shift, but lately my schedule’s been all over the place, and then there’s always some app notification or somebody needing something dropped across town. Half the time by the time I’m home I’m just… I don’t know, it’s late, and I’m thinking about whether I forgot to fuel up or if my phone battery’s going to make it tomorrow.

So have I lost interest? Maybe? I can’t really tell if I’m not interested or if I just haven’t been doing much.
Have these flashes and memories been affecting your relationships with friends or family?

Yeah… I mean, with friends and family, I don’t know if I’ve really been answering people much.

But the bigger thing is I’ve missed two shifts already, and that’s not like me. When I try to work, I just don’t feel safe driving around or handling deliveries. I get too shaken up, too on edge, and then I’m thinking about every little thing on the road, and it’s like—sorry, I know you asked about relationships.

I also stopped showing up for the volunteer stuff I usually do. Being around people right now, I just can’t really keep it together. So… yeah, it’s affecting things.
Have you had difficulty concentrating on your work or daily activities since these flashes started happening?

Concentrating? I mean… I don’t know. Work is already kind of a million tiny things, you know? Addresses, apartment codes, don’t block the loading zone, somebody texting “where are you,” and then traffic’s doing whatever traffic does.

So it’s hard to tell if it’s concentration exactly, or just… the whole day being messy. I’ve always had to keep a bunch of stuff in my head. Lately I guess I’ve been double-checking things more, but maybe that’s just because I don’t want to screw up.

Daily stuff, same thing. I’ll walk into the kitchen and forget why, but people do that, right? I’m not sure I’d say it’s because of the flashes. I haven’t really thought about it that way.
Do you think you're a worse person now because of what happened in that holding room?

I don’t… I don’t know if I’d say “worse person.” That’s kind of a big thing to say, right?

I mean, people say stuff like, “you did what you had to do,” or “it wasn’t your fault,” and I get that they’re trying to help, but then my brain just kind of wanders off into, like… what does “fault” even mean when everything’s happening fast and nobody’s acting normal?

Sorry. I’m not trying to dodge it. I guess I haven’t really decided what I think about myself now. Some moments I feel okay, like I’m just a guy trying to get through the day, and then other moments I’m… I don’t know. I don’t have a clean answer for that.
Have you felt like these experiences have significantly impacted your overall daily life or ability to function?

Yeah… yeah, I think it has. I mean, I keep wanting to say I’m managing, because I’m used to just pushing through stuff, but I’ve already missed two shifts, and I don’t really do that.

And when I try to work, it’s like… I’m supposed to be driving around, handling deliveries, watching traffic, parking, all that normal stuff, but I don’t feel safe doing it. I get too shaken up and on edge, and then every little thing on the road feels like too much.

And I stopped going to the volunteer thing too, which I usually show up for. I just… being around people right now, I can’t really keep it together. So, yeah, it’s definitely messing with my day-to-day.
Have you noticed any problems in your relationships with friends, family, or coworkers since these flashes and memories started?

Yeah… I mean, I guess it’s mostly my temper. Like, people aren’t doing anything that crazy and I’m snapping like they are.

Dispatch changed my schedule the other day—not even a huge thing, just moved stuff around—and I just… blew up. I was talking way louder than I needed to, like they’d personally screwed me over or something. And then at basketball, this guy bumped me, which happens every five seconds in basketball, right? Normally I’d just laugh it off or talk a little trash and keep playing, but I cursed him out. Like really went at him.

It’s weird because I don’t even feel like I’m trying to start problems. It just comes out fast, and then I’m standing there thinking, what was that? So yeah, I think people have been getting the rough side of me lately.
Do you believe you're a bad person because of what happened in the holding room?

I don’t know. “Bad person” feels… I mean, I hear that and it sounds like something you say about somebody who meant to do something, you know?

But then I keep turning it over anyway. Like when I was a kid, my uncle used to say you find out who somebody really is when things get ugly, and I hated that saying because he used it for everything—traffic, bills, like whatever—and now it keeps popping into my head at the worst times.

So… I don’t know if I believe I’m bad. I don’t think I can say that straight out. But I also don’t feel normal about myself when I think about that room. It’s like I can’t land on an answer.
Do you think you're worthless or a bad person because of what happened in that holding room?

I mean… I don’t know. Worthless feels like a big word. I don’t usually talk about myself like that, or I try not to.

Bad person… I keep getting stuck on that one more. Like, I can’t tell if what happened says something about me, or if I’m just making it into that because my head won’t leave it alone. It’s like when you replay an argument in the shower and suddenly you’re mad all over again, except this isn’t some dumb argument, you know? Sorry, that’s not really the question.

I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure. I don’t walk around saying, “I’m worthless.” But I don’t feel good about myself when I think about that room. I can’t really sort it out cleanly.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including intrusive memories and flashes of a traumatic event, avoidance of triggers that remind them of the event, difficulty sleeping, and feeling on edge or easily startled, are consistent with Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
